title: Secrets rotation and audit runbook — KMS/HSM integration for private deployments (v0.1 draft)
content:
Purpose
This document is an operator-oriented runbook for secrets rotation, key lifecycle, and audit log configuration when integrating cloud KMS and on-prem HSM into Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) deployments. It focuses on the concrete steps operators and infra engineers should follow when: onboarding a new customer, upgrading TF modules, rotating keys, and responding to suspected key compromise.

Scope and assumptions
- Targets: private deployments (VPC, private control plane, on-prem package).
- Assumes customers use either: cloud KMS (managed) reachable via VPC endpoints, or an HSM appliance integrated via KMIP or cloud HSM provider.
- Assumes Terraform is used to provision infra/config (we have a private-kms-module).
- Not covered: application-level secret design (covered elsewhere), full legal/compliance sign-off.

High-level architecture patterns
- Cloud KMS (recommended for most customers):
  - KMS in customer cloud account or a vendor-managed KMS with cross-account key grants.
  - Use private VPC endpoints for KMS APIs; avoid public egress for key operations.
  - Envelope encryption: data keys generated by KMS, used locally on inference nodes (never store plaintext).
- HSM-backed keys (required for FIPS / high-assurance customers):
  - HSM (on-prem or hosted) holds root key material; KMS or key-manager proxies wrap keys for service use.
  - Use KMIP or cloud vendor HSM integration; ensure low-latency connectivity between inference cluster and HSM gateway.

Operator runbook: onboarding a new private deployment
1) Preflight checklist (before TF apply)
   - Confirm customer network: CIDR ranges, VPC endpoints allowed, firewall rules for KMS/HSM ports, proxied egress.
   - Confirm KMS/HSM choice and ownership (customer-managed vs. redwood-managed).
   - Collect key policy requirements (who can decrypt/sign, audit requirements, rotation windows).
   - Confirm logging sink (CloudLogging/Splunk/Datadog) and SIEM integration point.

2) Terraform module notes (private-kms-module)
   - Key variables to set:
     - kms_provider = "gcp|aws|azure|onprem-hsm"
     - kms_key_alias = "redwood/private/<customer>"
     - kms_audit_logging = true/false
     - kms_endpoint_vpc = "com.amazonaws.vpce-..." (for providers that support VPC endpoints)
   - Outputs to consume:
     - cipher_key_id (string)
     - kms_endpoint_fqdn (string)
   - Typical resource pieces in module:
     - kms_key resource (provider-specific)
     - kms_key_policy with principal ARNs for operator roles + service agent role
     - IAM bindings or service accounts for the control plane to call Encrypt/Decrypt
     - VPC endpoint and route table attachment (if required)
   - Terraform upgrade notes: when bumping module version, run plan with -target to isolate KMS resources, avoid replace of keys. We should never force-replace a customer key without explicit migration steps.

Terraform snippet (example variable defaults):
```hcl
module "customer_kms" {
  source = "github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules/private-kms-module?ref=v0.3"
  kms_provider = var.kms_provider
  kms_key_alias = "redwood/private/${var.customer_id}"
  kms_audit_logging = true
}
```

3) Key provisioning flow (recommended)
   - For cloud KMS: create a customer-specific key with asymmetric or symmetric policy depending on use-case. Do NOT enable automatic key rotation unless customer wants 30/60/90-day cycles.
   - For HSM: perform key import ceremony (see notes below) or generate keys in HSM. Ensure key material never leaves HSM if required.
   - Store the key identifier and metadata in Redwood config store (encrypted by KMS) with restricted ACLs.

Secrets handling patterns
- Never store plaintext secrets in Git or TF state. Use remote state encryption and restrict state access.
- For runtime secrets (service credentials, DB passwords): store secrets encrypted with data keys and rotate the envelope key periodically.
- Use short-lived service tokens where possible; avoid static long-lived secrets.

Audit logs and observability
- What to log:
  - KMS Encrypt/Decrypt/Sign/Verify API calls (principal, timestamp, resource id).
  - Admin operations: key creation, rotation, policy changes, deletion/pending-deletion.
  - Key import/export operations (for HSM flows).
- Log routing:
  - Send KMS logs to a dedicated log project/account and forward to SIEM.
  - Tag logs with customer_id and deployment_id to enable per-customer filtering.
- Example log alert rules (baseline):
  - Unusual number of Decrypt calls > N in 5m window (possible exfil).
  - Key policy changed outside scheduled maintenance window.
  - Key scheduled for deletion (immediate operator notification).

Key rotation and migration plan
- Rotation cadence guidance: default 90 days for envelope keys, 1–3 years for root/HSM keys unless policy requires stricter.
- Rotation steps (envelope key):
  1. Create new data key (GenerateDataKey API) using current KMS key.
  2. Re-encrypt stored secrets with new data key (background job with rate limiting).
  3. Update service config to accept both old and new keys during migration window.
  4. After verification, retire old key material and update documentation.
- Migration between providers (cloud -> HSM or HSM -> cloud):
  - Plan a staged migration: replicate encrypted assets, test decryption in staging, cutover DNS/IP-level, verify client connectivity, then revoke old keys.
  - Maintain a read-only compatibility layer for a minimum of 48 hours post-cutover.

Emergency response: suspected key compromise
1) Immediate actions:
   - Rotate affected keys (create replacement key and update service agents).
   - Quarantine deployment: block traffic from suspect hosts via ACLs.
   - Trigger incident playbook (PagerDuty, incident commander).
2) For HSM-based compromise: follow key-ceremony and forensic guidelines; do NOT import new keys until HSM integrity verified.
3) Communications: notify customer security and legal; provide timeline and scope of affected data.

Testing and compliance checks (pre-prod)
- Test cases to automate:
  - Decrypt/Encrypt roundtrip with rotated key during migration window.
  - Failure mode: KMS endpoint unreachable -> automatic fallback to cached data keys for read-only ops (with TTL).
  - Audit log pipeline failure -> buffer to local disk and forward when pipeline restored.
- Compliance artifacts to collect for audits: key policy snapshots, rotation history, key import logs, Terraform state snapshots (redacted).

Open questions / TODOs
- Should we standardize on envelope key TTL of 90d across all enterprise customers? (security vs. operational cost tradeoff).
- Define exact threshold N for Decrypt-call anomaly alerts per customer workload pattern.
- Add HSM import/export SOP to this runbook (linked: key-ceremony notes).

Appendix: HSM key ceremony quick notes
- Steps: create key in HSM (or import via split-wrapping), record key ID, capture audit log entries, distribute wrapped key shares to escrow vaults, update TF metadata.
- Operator caution: never include raw key material in Terraform variables.

References
- Internal: Confluence KMS Integration Runbook (linked in metadata)
- TF module: github.com/redwood-inference/terraform-modules/private-kms-module
- External: cloud vendor KMS audit logging docs (linked)

Changelog
- v0.1 (2025-02-12) initial draft — Jordan Patel
- v0.1.1 (2025-03-01) added Terraform upgrade guidance and emergency sequence — Lina Gomez

Notes to reviewers
- This is deliberately operator-facing; please add concrete terraform variable names and a worked example from a recent customer onboarding. Also flag any missing security/regulatory items we must escalate to legal/compliance.
